content: Carbohydrate digestion and absorption are essential biological processes that convert dietary starches and sugars into simpler monosaccharides—glucose, fructose, and galactose—that can be absorbed by the small intestine and used for energy. Digestion starts in the mouth with salivary amylase breaking down starch into smaller polysaccharides and continues primarily in the small intestine where pancreatic amylase further cleaves starch to maltose and other disaccharides. Brush border enzymes, such as maltase, sucrase, and lactase, then hydrolyze these disaccharides into monosaccharides. Glucose and galactose are absorbed into enterocytes mainly via active transport involving sodium-dependent glucose transporters, while fructose is absorbed through facilitated diffusion. These monosaccharides are then transported into the bloodstream to provide fuel for cells. Efficient carbohydrate digestion is critical for maintaining energy homeostasis and overall health. Limitations include enzyme deficiencies such as lactase deficiency leading to lactose intolerance. Understanding of carbohydrate digestion also relates to concepts of glycemic control and metabolic health. Practical guidance includes consuming a balanced diet rich in complex carbohydrates and awareness that some individuals may have impaired digestion due to enzyme insufficiencies or intestinal disorders.

content: Carbohydrates are one of the three major macronutrients in the human diet, providing a primary source of energy. They occur mainly as starches and sugars in foods, and their digestion is necessary for converting them into absorbable forms. This section introduces carbohydrate types and their dietary sources.

chunk_title: Initiation of Starch Digestion in the Mouth
content: Digestion of carbohydrates begins as soon as food enters the mouth. Salivary amylase acts on starch molecules, partially breaking them down into smaller polysaccharides and maltose. This initial step prepares carbohydrates for further digestion in the small intestine.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
chunk_title: Role of Pancreatic Amylase in the Small Intestine
content: Most starch digestion occurs in the small intestine through pancreatic amylase secreted into the duodenum. This enzyme further hydrolyzes starch into disaccharides such as maltose and limit dextrins, which brush border enzymes will subsequently process.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
chunk_title: Brush Border Enzymes and Disaccharide Breakdown
content: Enzymes located on the microvilli of the small intestine, such as maltase, sucrase, and lactase, finalize carbohydrate digestion by breaking disaccharides into the monosaccharides glucose, fructose, and galactose. This enzymatic activity enables the absorption of simple sugars.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
chunk_title: Absorption of Monosaccharides in the Small Intestine
content: Glucose and galactose are absorbed into intestinal cells mainly through active transport mechanisms involving sodium-dependent glucose transporter 1 (SGLT1). Fructose absorption occurs through facilitated diffusion via GLUT5 transporters. Inside enterocytes, monosaccharides exit into the bloodstream via GLUT2 transporters.

content: Efficient digestion and absorption of carbohydrates provide the cells of the body with a steady supply of glucose, an essential energy substrate. Disruptions in this process impact energy balance and can cause gastrointestinal symptoms or systemic metabolic effects.

chunk_title: Common Enzyme Deficiencies Impacting Carbohydrate Digestion
content: Lactase deficiency is prevalent in many populations and causes lactose intolerance symptoms such as bloating and diarrhea due to unabsorbed lactose in the colon. Other less common enzyme deficiencies can impair digestion of specific carbohydrates, affecting nutrient uptake and health.

chunk_title: Relation of Carbohydrate Digestion to Metabolic Health
content: Proper carbohydrate digestion influences blood glucose levels, glycemic control, and can affect the risk of metabolic conditions such as obesity and diabetes. Understanding the digestion process helps inform dietary strategies that promote metabolic health and prevent disease.
